paper_summary: LSU MSc thesis (K. Chittineni, 2009) on integrated functionally gradient syntactic foams (IFGSFs): four-layer DGEBA epoxy (D.E.R. 332 / GE-8 diluent / D.E.H. 24) foams in which each layer holds 60 vol% 3M Scotchlite glass microballoons of a different wall thickness (S22, S32, S38, K46), the layers being cast one over another and integrated before solidification instead of being adhesively bonded. Five layer sequences (S22-K46-K46-S22, K46-S22-S22-K46, S32-S38-S38-S32, S38-S32-S32-S38 and the unsymmetric K46-S38-S32-S22) were tested in flat-wise and edge-wise quasi-static compression and in drop-weight impact at 1, 2 and 3 m/s. IFGSFs absorb 210-280% more flat-wise energy than plain foam of similar density (stress plateau 8-60% strain vs 10-20%), raise edge-wise yield strength 25-40%, and beat adhesively bonded FGSF by 50% in yield strength and 75% in energy absorption; sequences with the denser layers in the centre absorb the most energy.

processing.matrix_name: DGEBA epoxy D.E.R. 332 (Dow) with 5 vol% Erisys GE-8 C12-C14 aliphatic mono-glycidyl ether diluent and 13 vol% D.E.H. 24 (TETA) hardener
processing.particle_grade: 3M Scotchlite K46/S22 glass microballoons, layer sequence S22-K46-K46-S22 (each layer 60 vol% microballoons)

structure.microstructure_notes: Four-layer integrated functionally gradient syntactic foam, layer sequence S22-K46-K46-S22, each layer 60 vol% microballoons; layers integrated before full solidification, vacuum 30-45 min. Microballoon properties (Table 1): S22 rho=220 kg/m3, eta=0.9703, wall 0.52 um, 35 um median dia.; S32 320 kg/m3, 0.9561, 0.88 um; S38 380 kg/m3, 0.9474, 1.05 um; K46 460 kg/m3, 0.9356, 1.29 um (S32/S38/K46 median dia. 40 um).

test.standard: ASTM C 365/C 365M-05 (flat-wise compression)
test.specimen_notes: Flat-wise quasi-static compression on MTS-810 servo-hydraulic machine, ~32x32x16 mm specimens, crosshead 1.3 mm/min (strain rate not stated), 5 specimens per configuration. Energy absorption = area under the stress-strain curve (MPa-mm/mm = MJ/m^3).

evidence.location: Table 6 (p. 35): Flat-wise compressive properties of plain and IFGSF configurations
Table 5 (p. 28): Measured densities and open cell porosity in FGSF configurations

records.sample_label: Adhesively bonded FGSF, same layer sequencing (comparison data from Gupta & Ricci, ref. [16])

processing.matrix_name: DGEBA epoxy D.E.R. 332 (Dow) with 5 vol% Erisys GE-8 C12-C14 aliphatic mono-glycidyl ether diluent and 13 vol% D.E.H. 24 (TETA) hardener
processing.particle_grade: Layered syntactic foam with the same layer sequencing as K46-S38-S32-S22, layers joined with adhesive
processing.additional_fillers: Adhesive bond layers between the syntactic foam layers

structure.microstructure_notes: Gradient foam whose layers are adhesively bonded rather than integrated while still liquid; peeling stresses at the adhesive interfaces.

test.specimen_notes: Flat-wise compression comparison data quoted from earlier work (Gupta et al. [16]), not measured here.

evidence.quote: It is evident that the compressive yield strength values have increased from around 32.7 MPa for adhesively bonded FGSF to 49 MPa for IFGSF, an increase of 50%. Additionally, it is found that the overall energy absorption of IFGSF (28.9 MPa-mm/mm) is found to be 75% more than the energy absorption of adhesively bonded FGSFs (16.5 MPa-mm/mm).

extraction_notes: 28 records = 6 flat-wise compression (Table 6: 5 IFGSF + plain foam), 6 edge-wise compression (Table 7), 15 drop-weight impact (Tables 8-10: 5 configurations x 3 velocities) and 1 secondary record for the adhesively bonded FGSF comparison quoted from Gupta & Ricci [16]. Energy absorption is reported as MPa-mm/mm, i.e. stress x strain, which equals MJ/m^3, so the values were carried into energy_absorption_mj_m3 unchanged. Densities from Table 5 were converted kg/m3 -> g/cm^3, and 'open cell porosity' (the matrix void content from mechanical mixing, as opposed to the closed porosity inside the microballoons) was converted from % to a fraction and stored as matrix_porosity_fraction. Table 5 gives separate specimen densities for the flat-wise and edge-wise coupons, and each is attached to the matching test; no density is tabulated for the impact coupons or for the plain foams, so those are null. IMPACT RECORDS CARRY NO PROPERTY VALUES: the schema has no field for initiation energy (J), propagation energy (J) or maximum contact load (kN), and converting them into MJ/m^3 or a stress would require inventing an effective volume/area, so the measured numbers are preserved verbatim in each record's evidence quote and in test.specimen_notes instead. Plain-foam impact values exist only as bars in Figs. 33-35 and 37-39 and were not read off. Strain rate is null everywhere: the compression tests state only a 1.3 mm/min crosshead speed. Test temperature was set to 25 C (ambient; not stated explicitly). For the four configurations built from two microballoon grades, particle_true_density_g_cc, mean diameter and radius ratio are left null because they differ layer by layer; the per-grade values from Table 1 are recorded in microstructure_notes. particle_volume_fraction = 0.60 is the constant per-layer microballoon loading. cure_or_process_temperature_c = 100 C is the 3 h post-cure (24 h room-temperature cure first). Note that Table 1's wall thicknesses (0.52, 0.88, 1.05, 1.29 um) are about half those quoted for the same 3M grades in other theses from this group; the values are reproduced as printed. The plain-foam comparison samples were fabricated in this study (hence primary) but their microballoon grade is not stated.
